reason: The sources provide multi-site corroboration for 18 atomic facts covering the launch strikes, telemetry recovery, and landing.
story: On November 14, 1969, Apollo 12 launched into a rainy Florida sky with President Richard Nixon watching from the stands. Just 36.5 seconds into flight, a bolt of lightning struck the Saturn V rocket, followed by a second strike at 52 seconds. The spacecraft itself had triggered the bolts, acting like a giant flying lightning rod. Inside the command module, all three fuel cells disconnected, the cockpit became a blinding wall of warning lights, and Mission Control's telemetry turned into total gibberish. While the Saturn V's independent guidance system kept the rocket flying true, the spacecraft seemed doomed. In Houston, 26-year-old flight controller John Aaron recognized the telemetry failure pattern from an obscure test and called out, 'Try SCE to Aux.' Neither the flight director nor the commander knew what the switch was, but lunar module pilot Alan Bean found it, flipped it, and restored telemetry, saving the mission to the Moon.
angle: The Apollo 12 rocket was not hit by random storm lightning; the 363-foot rocket and its ionized exhaust plume actually created the lightning bolts that nearly destroyed it.

claims.claim: Apollo 12 launched on November 14, 1969, from Launch Pad 39A at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
The mission crew was Commander Charles 'Pete' Conrad Jr., Command Module Pilot Richard F. Gordon, and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean.
President Richard Nixon attended the liftoff, marking the first time a sitting U.S. president witnessed a crewed space launch.
The Saturn V rocket was struck by lightning twice during its first minute of flight.
The first lightning strike hit the rocket 36.5 seconds after liftoff.
The first lightning strike knocked all three fuel cells offline, forcing the spacecraft onto battery power.
A second lightning strike hit the vehicle 52 seconds after liftoff.
The lightning strikes scrambled telemetry transmissions sent to Mission Control into unreadable data.
The Saturn V rocket's internal guidance system in the Instrument Unit operated independently from the spacecraft and was unaffected by the strikes.
The lightning discharges were triggered by the rocket itself as its conductive metal body and ionized exhaust plume traveled through charged clouds.
EECOM flight controller John Aaron recognized the corrupted telemetry pattern from a prior test.
Aaron issued the instruction 'Try SCE to Aux' to switch the Signal Conditioning Equipment to auxiliary power.
Lunar Module Pilot Alan Bean located the obscure switch and flipped it to auxiliary, restoring readable data to Mission Control.
The crew manually brought the fuel cells back online and verified the spacecraft was healthy in Earth orbit.
Apollo 12 became the first crewed spaceflight to fly a hybrid non-free-return lunar trajectory.
Conrad and Bean executed a precision landing in the Ocean of Storms on November 19, 1969.
The Lunar Module landed within walking distance of the Surveyor 3 robotic probe that arrived in 1967.
Apollo 12 deployed an Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package powered by a SNAP-27 plutonium generator.
Apollo 12 completed its mission on November 24, 1969, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean where the crew was recovered by the USS Hornet.

disputed: Fate of the Saturn V third stage (S-IVB): S2 states that after failing to reach heliocentric orbit, the S-IVB remained in Earth orbit for 42 days before burning up in the atmosphere; S1 states it stayed in semi-stable Earth orbit until 1971, escaped into solar orbit, briefly returned in 2002 as object J002E3, and remains in solar orbit. A script should leave out the post-Apollo fate of the S-IVB.

Context of Aaron's earlier observation: S4 attributes Aaron's prior encounter to a flight simulation, while S5 notes accounts differ between a Cape ground test and a simulation, noting Aaron remembered a spacecraft test. A script should neutrally phrase it as 'an earlier test or simulation'.
